summary: An 80-ft steel tower built by CCC crews in 1936 on Mount Dunlap, Franklin County; now fenced off and used for radio equipment.

facts.design: 80-ft steel lookout tower, Aermotor MC-39 per the register (1936)

access.note: Closed off by a fence; used for communications equipment. Owned by Washington Township since 2004.

visit.trail_note: The Appalachian Trail passes a bit below the summit.

events.note: State forest service begins using the knob as a lookout; early observations from birch trees at the summit
Boy Scout troop builds a log cabin for the state forest fire warden
Steel tower erected by CCC crews from Camp S-70 at the Old Forge; purchased with emergency conservation work funds
CCC builds access roads and a stone observer cabin about 100 feet from the tower
Towerman spots a forest fire said to have destroyed about 75 acres of timberland in Mt. Alto State Forest; the item is credited to The Morning Herald, not the Waynesboro paper
State offers the stone cabin at the site for sale and asks that it be demolished and removed by July 1, 1966
A 19-year-old from Waynesboro falls from the tower and dies
Tower not staffed in fall 1973 because the Snowy Mountain lookout was back in service
Tower serves as a communications tower for Washington Township
Washington Township buys the tower and about an acre from a church that used it for a radio antenna
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register as US 985

corrections.why: The register and the 1936 papers both say 80 feet (about 24.4 m). The 27.4 m figure (90 ft) matches only the Penn State page, which conflicts with the other sources.

notes_for_editor: Height is disputed: 80 ft (register, 1936 papers), 90 ft (Penn State page, 2015), and a 110 ft survey estimate reported by Willhite. facts.height_m is already 24.4 (80 ft, per the register and the 1936 papers), which is what the story uses. The corrections entry records the earlier 27.4 m value, which matches only the 90 ft figure. Ownership and fence status come from the register and Willhite (2004 purchase); no source here confirms the current condition. Staffing info ends in 1973. The Willhite page reports a 1973 fatal fall; the story names no one. Do not encourage climbing: the tower is fenced.
